connector: At the end of Chapter 4, an iron weight meant for a runaway struck Harriet instead, and she was badly hurt. Chapter 5 follows her through a long, slow healing. Master wants to sell her, and two traders decide she is “not worth sixpence.” Track what Harriet does next, and in what order, and ask what those traders failed to see about her.

a.raw: harriets gourd grew heavier each week but masters price was far higher than her savings
a.fixed: Harriet’s gourd grew heavier each week, but Master’s price was far higher than her savings.
a.why: Capital H on Harriet’s, and apostrophe-s shows the gourd belongs to her; capital M and apostrophe-s on Master’s; a comma before but joins two complete thoughts; heavier and higher are comparative adjectives.

b.raw: harriets gourds grew lighter each month but johns spending grew larger
b.fixed: Harriet’s gourds grew lighter each month, but John’s spending grew larger.
b.why: Capital H on Harriet’s, and apostrophe-s shows the gourds are hers; capital J and apostrophe-s on John’s; a comma before but joins two complete thoughts; lighter and larger are comparative adjectives.

fill1.h1: Long before phones, a message could zip down a wire to a town miles away. Which part means far?
fill1.why: tele- means far: tele + graph = writing sent from far away.

fill2.h1: You can hear the voice of someone across the country. Which part means far?
fill2.why: tele- means far: tele + phone = sound carried from far away.

fill3.h1: A famous person signs their own name for a fan. Which part means self?
fill3.why: auto- means self: auto + graph = self-writing, your own signature.

fill4.h1: This vehicle moves by itself, with no horse to pull it. Which part means self?
fill4.why: auto- means self: auto + mobile = self-moving, a car.

eg: Each week, Harriet saved a few pennies from her pay.

notes.wgrd: A biography moves through time. Watch for time words like soon, on Christmas Day, and by spring. Put the events in order: what happened first, and what did it lead to next?
vocab: The order in which events happened, from first to last.
A personal account of what someone has seen or done.
The act of being set free.
notes.wordParts: tele- means “far” or “far away,” and auto- means “self”: telegraph, telescope, autograph, and autobiography.
notes.grammar: A comparative adjective compares two things. Short adjectives add -er: thinner, weaker, stronger. Longer ones use more instead: more hopeless, more careful.
notes.spelling: The suffix -ion turns a verb into a noun: inspect becomes inspection, express becomes expression. Sometimes the verb’s ending changes first: decide becomes decision.

transcripts.welcome: Hey, it’s Marcus. Chapter 4 ended with Harriet badly hurt, struck by an iron weight that was meant for a runaway. Chapter 5 is called Not Worth a Sixpence. When I first read that title, it made me angry, because somebody says those words about Harriet. Today’s question: what do they miss about her? And who is she becoming while nobody is paying attention?
transcripts.guide2: Freedom Watch: the strength nobody planned for. Master and the men who come to look at Harriet only see her worth in dollars. But during the long months in the cabin, something changes inside her that nobody can measure. In my research, this is the part I keep coming back to. Watch for the moment Sterling tells you how Harriet sees herself now.
transcripts.read: Chapter 5 covers a lot of time, so watch the time words: holidays, seasons, even a year. Track how Harriet’s strength comes back, one step at a time. Notice where she keeps her money, and count it as it grows. Later you’ll meet someone new on the courthouse steps in Cambridge. I’ve walked those Cambridge streets. Read that part closely.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: something far away, or something done by itself?

why.t: In Chapter 5, Harriet sews a patchwork quilt of her own. By the fire at night, she pieces together scraps of cloth until it is as warm and beautiful as her mother’s. On hard nights, she pulls it around her shoulders and looks for the North Star through the cracks in the roof. tele- means far, and auto- means self. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: Harriet’s quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. tele- = far, auto- = self.
